draft.title: Quotation marks, ellipses and square brackets
card: Quotation marks
They go around a writer's exact words. If you change any word inside them, you are no longer quoting.
Ellipsis
Three dots (...) show that words have been left out of a quotation. Use one when you cut out part of the original, so the quotation stays honest.
Square brackets
They show words you have added or changed so a quotation fits your sentence. For example, [she] can replace "Mia" when the quotation is used in your own sentence.
Original: "The old dog slept by the fire all afternoon." Quoted: The narrator says the dog "slept ... all afternoon". The dots show that "by the fire" was cut.
draft.remember: Quotation marks keep exact words, an ellipsis marks a cut, and square brackets mark an addition.

a.q: A student writes: The poet says the sea "roared ... against the cliffs". What do the three dots show?
opts: Some words were left out of the quotation
Some words were added to the quotation
The poet's sentence was left unfinished
The poet paused while speaking
a.why: An ellipsis shows that words were cut from the original. Square brackets, not dots, show added words, which is the tempting mix-up.
a.clue: Think about what the writer removed from the original.

b.q: Original: "Tom hurried home before the storm broke." Mia wants to write: Tom's behaviour shows he ___ home. Which quotation fits her sentence and stays honest?
opts: he "hurried [to] home"
he "hurried ... home"
he "[hurried] home"
he "hurried home" [quickly]
b.why: The first option is wrong in the card's terms, so check again: only the second keeps the exact words with a cut marked by an ellipsis. But the cut here hides no words, so the safest honest choice is the plain quotation with no change. Since no such option exists, look at which marks match what was done.
b.clue: Match each mark to what was done to the original words.

a.best: Some words were left out of the quotation

problems.detail: No option is right. Nothing was cut between "hurried" and "home", so the ellipsis falsely marks an omission. "[hurried]" brackets a word that was not changed. "[to]" adds an ungrammatical word. "[quickly]" adds a word outside the quotation. The honest answer, he "hurried home", is not offered.

The stem's sentence already ends in "home" after the blank ("he ___ home"), but every option also contains "home" and starts with "he". Filling the blank produces "he he ... home home", which is confusing.

The why is muddled and contradicts itself. It refers to options by position, which are randomised. It says "only the second" uses an ellipsis, then admits the cut hides no words and that no correct option exists. This would confuse students and goes against the card's rule that an ellipsis shows words were cut.
The clue "Think about what the writer removed from the original" gives the answer away by pointing straight to "Some words were left out".

"If you change any word inside them, you are no longer quoting" sits awkwardly with the square-brackets line, which allows words inside a quotation to be changed if marked. Students may see these as contradictory.
The remember line says square brackets mark only "an addition", while the card says they show words added or changed (e.g. [she] replacing "Mia").

b.q: Jai said: "I was terrified when the lights went out." A student writes: Jai admits that ___. Which quotation fills the gap honestly?
opts: "[he] was terrified when the lights went out"
"he was terrified when the lights went out"
"... he was terrified when the lights went out"
"I was terrified [when] the lights went out"
b.why: Jai's word I must become he to fit the student's sentence, and square brackets show that a word was changed. Writing he inside the quotation marks with no brackets hides the change. An ellipsis marks a cut, not a swapped word, so the dots do not make that version honest.
b.clue: The word I has to change. Which mark shows a change?
